summary:
Lunar Margin helps lunar mission planners compare locations and arrival times to find sunlight for solar power and a clear view of Earth for direct communication. Near the Moon's south pole, hills and crater rims can block both.

Our browser app connects NASA terrain and JPL position data to a rotatable Moon, local 3D terrain, a 2D horizon and aligned Sun/Earth timelines. Users set visibility limits, see which locations fit, inspect what blocks a view, and try another location or arrival while keeping their requirements.

It compares five documented lunar locations and study points across 2026, with additional regional custom-coordinate calculations. Optional tools estimate battery cover from user inputs and show NASA Diviner thermal and ice-stability context. A short guide and mobile layout make the calculations easier to explore.
details:
Lunar Margin helps mission planners, educators and the public understand how a lunar location and arrival date affect access to sunlight and direct communication with Earth.

Solar-powered landers need sunlight to generate electricity. Direct-to-Earth communication requires an unobstructed view of Earth. Near the Moon’s south pole, both can appear close to the horizon, where hills and crater rims can interrupt visibility for long periods.

We built Lunar Margin to make these constraints easier to explore and explain. Users can compare locations, set their own requirements, change arrival dates and inspect the terrain behind each result. The app connects the question “Does this visit meet my requirements?” with “Why?” and “What could I try next?”

PLANNING A VISIT

Users choose an arrival date in UTC and a length of stay. The app provides common stay lengths and an option to enter another duration in hours.

Users then set three visibility requirements:

• The longest continuous period they can accept without Sun visibility.

• The longest continuous period they can accept without Earth visibility.

• The minimum continuous period they need with both visible.

The results show the calculated duration beside each requirement, whether it passes, and how far it is above or below the limit. These checks use uninterrupted stretches of time. Separate expandable totals help users distinguish a continuous window from hours accumulated across several intervals.

Users can select a location for closer inspection or open a table comparing all available locations. Unknown results are distinguished from confirmed passes. Changes that have not yet been applied are identified, and outdated results are hidden while new inputs need checking or calculation. An undo control lets users restore the previous applied visit.

THE INTERACTIVE “SHOW ME HOW” GUIDE

The guide is designed for someone opening the app without prior space knowledge. It is an interactive walkthrough using the app’s actual controls, calculations and visualizations.

It follows three steps:

1. Set requirements.

The guide introduces a seven-day example visit and explains the three limits: at most 12 continuous hours without Sun visibility, at most 72 without Earth visibility, and at least 24 continuous hours with both visible. It explains that these are illustrative user requirements, chosen before comparing results.

2. Change the arrival while keeping the limits.

Users check the 14 November 2026 arrival and see whether any location meets all three requirements. The guide then keeps Athena’s location, the seven-day stay and the same requirements, while moving arrival one day later. This demonstrates the effect of changing arrival without making the requirements easier.

3. Inspect the result.

The guide explains the updated result and provides an action to inspect a calculated blocked interval in the visual workspace. Users can connect the reported duration to its time, body direction and terrain explanation.

In this example, moving arrival from 14 November to 15 November changes Athena’s modelled longest Sun-hidden stretch from 30.5 to 6.5 hours, allowing all three visibility checks to pass.

The guide shows progress, allows restarting, and can be exited at any stage. Finishing or exiting restores the user’s previous visit, selected location and requirements. It also explains what to explore next: compare another location, inspect a blockage or use “If your arrival slips” to investigate later options.

A separate short introduction explains why sunlight and Earth visibility matter. The guide makes clear that meeting visibility limits does not establish landing safety.

CONNECTED MOON AND TERRAIN VIEWS

The selected location and visit keep the comparison and visual workspace synchronized. Users can move between three views:

• 3D Moon: a rotatable, zoomable Moon with location markers. Selecting a marker connects the location to its comparison and terrain view. Controls focus the sites or frame Earth and Moon, or Sun and Moon.

• Local terrain: a rotatable view of the selected location’s surroundings, with Sun and Earth direction arrows and the calculated horizon relationship.

• 2D horizon: a simpler view of Sun and Earth positions relative to the local terrain horizon.

The whole-Moon view establishes geographic context. The local terrain and 2D horizon help explain the visibility calculation at the selected point.

Earth is incorporated through its calculated position, visibility results, direction arrows, timeline and globe representation. The globe uses Earth’s relative size and separation from the Moon. The displayed Sun is reduced and brought closer so it can fit within the visualization.

Local terrain settings allow users to switch between true-scale height and a clearly labelled exaggerated view for easier inspection. Users can also choose terrain relief or registered Moon Trek imagery where available. Imagery is available for the two original mission locations; the additional points use terrain relief.

TIME CONTROLS AND PAIRED TIMELINES

Two aligned timelines show Sun and Earth visibility over the same visit. Filled and outlined segments distinguish visible and hidden periods, while unknown periods are identified separately.

One moving time marker connects both timelines to the viewing-time input and direction arrows. Users can play through the visit, scrub the timeline, move forward or backward in 30-minute steps, or return to arrival.

The app also displays Sun and Earth elevations, current visibility states and upcoming visibility changes within the available data. Supported changes can be inspected directly. Users can inspect hidden intervals or move to the next time both bodies are visible within the visit.

INSPECTING WHAT BLOCKS A VIEW

A “Show why” action links a failed requirement to the relevant calculated interval. Users can inspect the interval’s start or last sample and return to the comparison.

The inspection explains whether the selected body clears or falls below the terrain horizon and shows its angular clearance. It identifies the limiting terrain point and indicates when that point lies beyond the displayed local patch.

An expandable terrain cross-section follows the selected body’s bearing and includes the limiting point. Additional evidence shows the viewing time, azimuth, elevation and calculated terrain horizon. This connects the result to an inspectable geometric explanation.

ALTERNATIVE ARRIVALS AND LOCATIONS

When a visit misses the requirements, Lunar Margin presents supported alternatives and explains what changes. Users can inspect other options and apply a suggested visit directly.

The “If your arrival slips” feature searches later available arrivals while keeping the stay length and requirements unchanged. An option may use the same location or another location that fits. For calculated visits, searches can extend up to 14 days after the selected arrival where source coverage permits.

The interface identifies when an option changes the location and shows the search’s date limits. Where requirements would need to change, the adjustment is shown explicitly. Suggestions are limited to the available locations, dates and model.

DOCUMENTED LOCATIONS AND DATE COVERAGE

The app includes five documented lunar points:

• IM-2 Athena’s reported landing location.

• IM-1 Odysseus’s reported landing location.

• Malapert Site 030, a published research candidate.

• The Malapert Crater 1 study-region centre.

• The Malapert Massif study-region centre.

The region centres represent study areas rather than selected landing points. The two Malapert Massif references are nearby points within the same area. Dates entered into Lunar Margin describe planning scenarios, not reconstructions of the spacecraft missions.

For these five points, the app supports half-hour arrival times throughout 2026 and stays from half an hour to 28 days, provided the visit ends by 1 January 2027. Windows outside the initially loaded dates calculate on demand in the browser. Date coverage is displayed, and unsupported visits are identified.

CUSTOM-COORDINATE CALCULATIONS

Users can enter their own latitude and longitude within the supplied south-polar terrain region. The custom-coordinate tool calculates visibility using the same terrain basis, observer height and exact-bearing method as the documented locations.

This tool has separate 12–24 November 2026 coverage. A coordinate must have sufficient surrounding terrain for the required horizon calculation; unsupported points are rejected explicitly.

Users can follow calculation progress, cancel a download or calculation, compare the result with the documented points, and inspect it in 3D. Custom results can be saved in the browser, exported as JSON and imported into another browser. A custom link alone does not transfer the saved calculation.

POWER AND BATTERY ESTIMATES

The power panel connects the longest Sun-hidden interval to a simplified battery question: how long could the supplied battery support a constant electrical load?

Users enter the load, nominal battery capacity and usable fraction. An optional published nominal spacecraft reference is available, with its limitations explained.

The estimate helps users explore battery coverage. It does not include charging, variable loads, temperature effects or a complete mission energy budget.

WATER-ICE AND RESOURCE CONTEXT

The resource panel presents thermal and modelled ice-stability context at the five documented points. Users can consider these environmental conditions alongside sunlight and Earth visibility.

The panel distinguishes conditions that could support ice stability from evidence of an actual deposit. It does not claim confirmed water ice, recoverable quantities or resource accessibility.

DETAILED ANALYSIS AND EXPORT

The detailed analysis view provides further arrival comparisons, terrain and horizon inspection, visibility information and calculation evidence.

Users can export supported results as JSON for further examination. Custom-coordinate calculations have their own export and import workflow, while calculated calendar visits can also be downloaded. The exports preserve relevant inputs, results and provenance information.

USABILITY AND LOADING

The main desktop workspace places the visualization beside the comparison. Draggable dividers let users adjust its width and height. Mobile uses a vertical layout with touch-sized controls.

The prominent “Show me how” action helps newcomers begin, while “Detailed analysis & export” remains easy to find for users who want more depth. Technical explanations are grouped into expandable sections.

The viewer opens with a lightweight initial dataset, then automatically preloads the five locations’ terrain evidence, meshes and available imagery in the background. Users do not have to select each location to start that loading. Loading states and retry controls identify incomplete downloads. The original models, textures and scientific values are preserved.

CALCULATION BASIS AND INTERPRETATION

Lunar Margin combines NASA lunar topography with calculated JPL Sun and Earth positions. The terrain calculation uses a native 120 m elevation grid, an observer 2 m above the surface and terrain checks extending up to 200 km, including lunar curvature.

Visibility is evaluated at 30-minute intervals by comparing each body’s centre with the calculated terrain horizon. Finer computational sampling interpolates the original terrain grid; it does not create higher-resolution measurements.

The comparison, arrows, timelines and inspection views use connected calculation records, with consistency checks to detect mismatched data versions.

The app is a planning and educational prototype. Terrain resolution, half-hour sampling, body-centre geometry and the finite search distance limit its conclusions. Global lighting is illustrative, and photographic terrain shadows do not change with the selected time. Position checks have been performed, but terrain-blocked hours have not been independently validated against a matching NASA result for the exact coordinates, dates and observer height.

For mission teams, the intended value is making early location-and-date trade-offs easier to communicate across scientific and engineering backgrounds. For educators and the public, the guide and connected views make the same constraints accessible to exploration.

Meeting the selected visibility requirements means that the model passes those checks. It does not establish sufficient electrical power, a working radio link, thermal survival or landing safety.
